maths.factorisation_techniques.subject: Mathematics
maths.factorisation_techniques.name: Factorisation techniques

importance.summary: Feeds the Algebra section every year (30/100 Gr 10, 45/150 Gr 11, 25/150 Gr 12 on Paper 1) AND Gr 12 Differential Calculus.

maths.factorisation_techniques.prior_knowledge: Products of binomials; HCF; difference of squares

diagnostic.prompt: What comes FIRST in any factorisation?
options: Take out the highest common factor

maths.factorisation_techniques.recap:
Factorising is unmultiplying: writing an expression as a product of brackets. Always work in the same order.

1. HCF first — every time. 3x² − 12 becomes 3(x² − 4) before you do anything else. Missing the HCF is the single most common lost mark.

2. Count the terms. TWO terms: look for a difference of squares a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), or a sum/difference of cubes. THREE terms: a trinomial — find two numbers that multiply to give ac and add to give b, then split and group. FOUR terms: group in pairs and pull a common bracket.

3. Check inside the brackets — a bracket like (x² − 4) can often be factorised again. "Factorise fully" means keep going until nothing factorises.

Multiply your brackets back out mentally; if you don't land on the original expression, a sign is wrong.

geography.contour_reading.subject: Geography
geography.contour_reading.name: Reading contour lines

importance.summary: Mapwork is Question 3 on BOTH Geography papers, every year: 30/150 per paper in Gr 11 and Gr 12 - contour reading is the entry point.

covered_by.topic: Consolidation of Grade 8 and 9 map skills

geography.contour_reading.example_problem: On a 1:50 000 extract with a 20 m contour interval, identify the river valley, the steepest slope and the highest point.
geography.contour_reading.recap:
Contour lines join points of equal height; the pattern they make IS the landscape.

Spacing = steepness: close together is steep, far apart is gentle, evenly spaced is a uniform slope.

Shapes: V-shapes pointing UPHILL mark a river valley (the stream flows out of the V). Rounded U-shapes pointing downhill are spurs. Closed rings are hills; the innermost ring is the summit area. A ridge reads as a long, narrow band of rings.

Heights: read the labelled contours and count intervals — on a 20 m interval map, three lines above the 200 m contour is 260 m. The highest possible point inside a closed ring is just under one interval above its value.

exit_check.prompt: Contour V-shapes point upstream. The river flows…
On a 20 m interval map, a point two contours above the 300 m line is…

geography.gradient_calculation.subject: Geography
geography.gradient_calculation.name: Gradient calculation

importance.summary: A named mapwork calculation: part of Question 3's map skills and calculations (10 of the 30 mapwork marks on each paper) and required for fluvial/geomorphology cross-section work.

geography.gradient_calculation.example_problem: Calculate the average gradient between trig beacon 251 (1 200 m) and a spot height of 900 m, 4.5 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map.
geography.gradient_calculation.prior_knowledge: Contour reading; map scale; unit conversion

diagnostic.prompt: Gradient between two points is expressed as…
options: Vertical interval : horizontal equivalent, as 1 : n

geography.gradient_calculation.recap:
Gradient answers one question: how steep is the slope between two points?

1. Vertical interval (VI): subtract the lower height from the higher one — trig beacon 1 200 m and spot height 900 m give VI = 300 m.

2. Horizontal equivalent (HE): measure the map distance between the points and convert with the scale. On a 1:50 000 map, 4.5 cm × 50 000 = 225 000 cm = 2 250 m.

3. Divide: gradient = VI : HE = 300 : 2 250. Reduce to 1 : n by dividing both sides by the VI → 1 : 7.5.

Always give the answer as 1 : n, keep units the same (both in metres) and show VI and HE — the mark allocation rewards the working, not just the ratio.

exit_check.prompt: VI = 300 m, map distance 4.5 cm on a 1:50 000 map. The gradient is…
A gradient of 1 : 3 compared to 1 : 30 is…
